M-007: Utopia - Presented by: Rob Lime
How do you handle sales calls when no pain is shared?
Utopia - When it seems impossible to get pain from a prospect, Utopia is a creative way to uncover it.
When to Use Utopia
At the end of your 30 second commercial - (when you could not find pain)
When nothing is happening
When your prospect is blowing lots of smoke

Types of Utopia Statements - “A” statements - Used first to paint the picture of perfection. If they agree then go on to the next “A” statement. - “B” statements - Used only after they disagree with your “A” statement.
Examples - A: You’re making more money than you ever dreamed possible. - Prospect disagrees - B: But more than last year, though.
Examples - A: And you are closing everybody. - Prospect disagrees - B: But almost everybody.
Examples - A: And you are getting appointments with more people than you can see. - Prospect disagrees - B: But you’re staying busy.
Examples - A: And you are doing this all in 15 hours a week. - Prospect disagrees - B: But no overtime, though.
Examples - A: And you are having the time of your life. - Prospect disagrees - B: But it isn’t horrible.
Why do you need “B” statements?
“B” Statements
Your prospect will be very uncomfortable the first time they have to admit to a problem.
You let them off the hook by saying your “B” statement
It will get them comfortable enough to keep going.
The goal is to get them to admit as many as possible.
Utopia
Intro: - After 30 second commercial: - “That’s great, sounds like everything is perfect.”

Transition: - “I have a lot of really happy customers who say everything is perfect just like you, so I would assume that the following things are true for you, too…” - Go into your ”A” Utopia statement
Ending: - This has to be well padded so start with: - Can I ask you a question without you getting mad at me? - Are you sitting down? - Can you sit any lower?

Identifying Decision Makers - WHAT ARE THE DIFFERENT ROLES WITHIN COMPANIES THAT - INFLUENCE THE PROCESS?

The Economic Buyer - Their budget consists of line items. They want to make sure that the dollar is well spent because they won’t have an opportunity to make it right later. - Concerns: - Budget fully utilized - Services - Back End Costs - Maintenance Costs - Billing Issues

The Influencer Group - They are affected by whatever product or service you are selling. They have a lot of power and can choose many different channels to get things done. - Concerns: - Make me look good - Improve situation without raising budget - Put our efforts in better light

The User Group - These people can’t have or don’t have the budget; however, they have the ultimate responsibility to make the project work. - Concerns: - Easy to Use - Make my job easier - Save Time - Easy to Learn

Rules to remember - There is a difference between selling and negotiation. - Pain is the trump card for all negotiations. - Keep the prospect ok. - Money is never the real issue. - Always keep your emotions in check.
Rule: - When negotiating, know your walk away point and be ok with going there if needed.
What negotiating tactics have you experienced?
Gambit: The Flinch
Why it works? - Because of parent/child response. - Sales people cower and comply.
Defense/prevention - Put the flinch in for them. - Gave the best deal we could. - Willingness to walk away.
Gambit: Your competition is cheaper
Why it works? - Creates emotional involvement in the sales person.
Defense/prevention - Early budget step hint at higher price. - Find a pain your competition can’t fix.
Gambit: Lower authority/higher authority
Why it works? - They can accept concessions but can not make any. - Sunk cost you have invested and don’t want to lose.
Defense/Prevention - Don’t negotiate with those who can not offer concessions. - 3rd party horror stories involving too much work in future.
Gambit: Good cop/bad cop
Why it works? - Creates a flinch from someone else. - Forces you to deal with someone’s objections indirectly.
Defense/prevention - Have your own bad cop.
Gambit: Hot potato
Why it works? - Sunk cost/emotional investment.
Defense/prevention - Have a strong post sell for things that could go wrong. - Toss the potato back. - Resist the concession.
Gambit: Fait Accompli
Why it works? - Timing and laziness from the sales person.
Defense/prevention - Add when they add, do what they do to you.
Gambit: Best and final offer
Why it works? - Creates emotional involvement
Defense/prevention - Are you the finalist or still competing? - If you give the price, are they committed to taking it? - Ask them to define what "best is". Best value, best delivery....
Gambit: Stonewalling
Why it works? - Sales rep starts to believe they are losing the deal due to no response.
Defense/prevention - Chinese menu through email.
Gambit: Nibbling
Why it works? - Small concessions are given and don’t realize full impact until too late/end.
Defense/prevention - Do not agree to anything unless you get something in return. - Always find out why they are asking for what they are before responding.
Gambit: Changing the rules
Why it works? - Sales reps don’t want to start over and want to preserve the work they have accomplished to date.
Defense/prevention - Get things in writing as early as possible. - Start over.
Gambit: Splitting the difference
Why it works? - Sales rep knows they are close to closing the sale.
Defense/prevention - Never offer this, let them make offers. When they are offering, they have already given up something.
Gambit: Have to do better
Why it works? - Evokes the parent/child response from the salesperson.
Defense/prevention - Define exactly what “do better” means.

Parent: Nurturing - Thoughts - Work hard, do your best, it will be OK - Feelings - Protective, loving, encouraging - Behavior - Smiling, open arms, concerned look, hugging

Child: Natural - Thoughts - I want, I wish, I can, let me - Feelings - Insecure, fun, loving, curious, inventive, rebellious, playful - Behavior - Laughter, pleading, tears, anger, joking
Child: Adaptive - Thoughts - Don’t leave me, love me, help me, show me - Feelings - Dependent, fearful, cautious - Behavior - Compliant, wrings hands, cowering, downcast eyes, people pleasing
Child: Rebellious - Thoughts - I want it my way - Feelings - Frustration, anger, rebellion - Behavior - Tantrums, pouting, sulking
Child: Little Professor - Thoughts - I will figure out how to get what I want - Feelings - Calm, unemotional, masking, passive agressivaggressive - Behavior - Manipulation, power

KEY RULE #1 - We view our way of being and way of acting as correct.

How to Identify Prospects’ Styles - It is a simple, three-step process of identifying your prospect's style: - Observe - Recognize - Assess
Observe

Step 1: Observe - When you meet a prospect, pay attention to traits such as: - "Types of words and questions... - "Body Language." - ...such as "I" vs "We" - or - "What the person talks about." - "What?" vs "Why?" - "Tonality"
Assess
Step 2: Assess - Determine if the prospect is more: - OR - Active - Reserved

If the prospect is Active, he/she is either D-style or I-style. - Talk about future and how things could be - Speak with a fairly loud voice and inflection - Demonstrate body language that is animated and assertive - Maintain strong eye-contact

If the prospect is Reserved, he/she is either S-style or C-style. - Talk about the present and past and how things are now - Speak with a calm and fairly quiet voice - Demonstrate body language that is limited - Tend to have hesitant eye-contact
Determine if the prospect is more: - OR - Task-Oriented - People -Oriented
If the prospect is Task-oriented, he/she is either D-style or C-style... - Talks and asks about things - Focuses more on tasks than people - Does not show a lot of emotion
If the prospect is People-oriented, he/she is either I-style or S-style... - Talks and asks about people - Focuses more on people than tasks - Shows emotion fairly easily
Recognize
Step 3: Recognize - Now you have the information needed to identify your prospect’s style by combining the Active-Reserved and - Task-People Orientation.

Step 3: Recognize - D-style = Active and Task-Oriented - Talks about: Goals, oneself, hard values ($, revenue, profits) results, change. - I-style = Active and People-Oriented - Talks about: People, team-spirit, good things, future, oneself - S-style = Reserved and People-Oriented - Talks about: Agreements, principles, past, proofs, one’s team - C-style = Reserved and Task-Oriented - Talks about: Facts, analyses, details, rules, instructions

How to Identify a D-style Prospect: - Take control of conversation - Direct and assertive - Fast-paced - Doesn't like to be micromanaged - Results-oriented - Little patience for fluff - Doesn't like deadlines - Interrupt conversations - Doesn't focus much on details

How to Identify an I-style Prospect: - Talks a lot - Animated - Open and friendly - Appears unorganized - Don't listen for long - Stays away from hard facts - Doesn't pay close attention - Jumps from subject to subject - Doesn't focus much on details

How to Identify an S-style Prospect: - Easy-going - Calm - Listens carefully - Appears thoughtful - Nods and goes along - "Let me think about it." - Likes own physical space - Not easily excited - Ponders alternatives, slow decision-making - Ask questions and inquire about specifics - Strong opinions, but not vocal - New ideas + things makes them uncomfortable

How to Identify an C-style Prospect: - Quiet - Focus on details - Proceeds cautiously - Asks many questions - Appears reserve and somewhat timid - Doesn't easily express disagreeing views - May have done homework on products and services - Studies specifications and other information carefully - Makes decisions after studying pertinent facts + issues - May be very critical; criticism based on facts, not opinion
D Styles

D-style Prospect - Motto: I did it my way. - Focus: Actively controls tasks and things. - Under Pressure: Lack of concern. - This refers to D-styles’ tendency to overlook how their actions and behaviors affect others. - Fear: Loss of control. - This refers to D-styles’ desire to be in charge. They do not want to give up control. - Favorite question: What? (What is the bottom line? - What is in it for me?)

D-style Prospect - Communication Style - Often to only one direction – he/she talks and expects others to listen - Expresses own opinions as facts that need no further discussion - May be blunt and challenges others - Interrupts others often

D-style Prospect - When communicating with a D-style prospect, remember to: - Be flexible to their ideas - Try to demonstrate you are their equal professionally, while letting them control the situation - Allow them to define the information they need - Let them make the decisions - Encourage them into positive consideration of all of the possibilities the product/service creates - Try to show them all of the new and exceptional things that you can offer - Provide the information, but let them discover the ideas

D-style Prospect - Tips on how to develop the relationship with a D-style client: - Be flexible to their changing needs and opinions - Show them that you appreciate their professional knowledge - Keep in regular contact, always offering them something useful - Even when they are wrong, let them win - Treat them as a unique individual and learn what they are interested in - Always plan together the next few steps - Contact them regularly so they do not have to contact you

D-style Prospect - With D-style prospects and clients, you do not... - Force them into deadlines - Be overly rigid on what was agreed to be done - Be too arrogant; you are still entitled to show you can defend your opinion - Try to control them - Prove them wrong - Let them forget that they are an important client to you - Try to prove everything wrong what they say

D-style Prospect - Moving the business relationship forward with D-style prospects and clients: - Prove them right - Make them believe that they know something you do not - Tell them something they have not thought about and let them discover what it means for them - Ask them if your suggestions would be good next steps - Ask them how they would like to start to use the product/service - Ask them directly if there is no point to continue - Make them believe that they are achieving something unique
I Styles

I-style Prospect - Motto: "I am a nice person. Everyone should like me." - Focus: Actively involved with other people and emotions - Under Pressure: Disorganized - This refers to I-styles' tendency to focus so much on people that they may overlook details and tasks. - Fear: Social rejection - This refers to I-styles' having a strong desire to be liked by others. - Favorite question: Who? (Who is going to be at the meeting? Who else is using this?)

I-Style Prospects - Communication Style: - Selling and inspiring - Talks a lot, but not about details - Avoids unpleasant subjects - Good at providing positive, constructive feedback - Not always direct

I-Style Prospects - When communicating with an I-style prospect, remember to: - Avoid using aggressive statements - Get them to tell stories - Support their dreams - do not start debating - Be friendly and open - Bring up important details but do not over-emphasize them - Show that you listen and care - Spend time small talking to create a friendly atmosphere

I-Style Prospects - Tips on how to develop the relationship with an I-style client: - Become their friend but do not expect anything from them - Be flexible to their needs - Always give them the credit - Remind them of you often, but in a non-demanding way - Let them shine in the limelight - Maintain regular contact with them - Make your friendship independent of your business relationship

I-Style Prospects - What not to do with I-style prospects and clients: - Do not engage them in anything that requires a lot of concentration - Do not try to control the meetings with them - Be careful not to underestimate their opinion - Be sure not to talk only about business - Do not disagree with them unnecessarily - Do not be blunt - Avoid making strong negative statements

I-Style Prospects - Moving the business relationship forward with I-style prospects and clients: - Be enthusiastic about the opportunity to work together - Do not pressure them but try to make buying easy and quick - Schedule your first follow-up visit before you have closed the sale - Get them to talk about something they like and then ask for the business - Mention a few trustworthy names during the conversation - Involve them with someone they value highly (if they sign the deal now) - If they start to bargain, accept their offer and close the deal
S Styles

S-style Prospect - Motto: "If it's not broken, let's not fix it." - Focus: Involved with familiar people. - Under Pressure: Too willing. - This refers to S-styles’ have a tendency to be accommodating and polite. Often they say “yes” too easily. - Fear: Loss of stability. - This refers to S-styles wanting to have a stable and secure environment. Change can be challenging for S-styles. - Favorite question: How? (How are we going to do this? How does this impact us?)

S-Style Prospects - Communication Style: - Often only to one direction, he/she listens - Answers when asked - Talks calmly - Creates trust - Talks about topics he/she masters - Better in one-to-one situations - Good instructor

S-Style Prospects - When communicating with an S-style prospect, remember to: - Do not start arguing about opinions - Do not disagree - let them decide - Spend time talking about general issues also - Earn their approval as their friend - Make them say what they want to achieve - Be careful not to push your own opinion onto them - Show your sincerity when talking about issues

S-Style Prospects - Tips on how to develop the relationship with an S-style client: - Give them new ideas as to how they can benefit from you, but do not force them to use them - Be flexible with them and always be prepared to help - Do not leave them alone when they need support - You need to trust them first before they will trust you - Do not invoice them for everything you do - Never debate about differences in opinions - Give them extra support when they are under pressure

S-Style Prospects - What not to do with S-style prospects and clients: - Do not forget to also talk about non-business issues - Do not behave aggressively - Be careful not to force them into accepting your opinion - Do not force them to a decision - Do not bring up anything they would consider additional risks; requiring further analysis - Do not disagree on issues that are important to them - Do not be too official

S-Style Prospects - Moving the business relationship forward with S-style prospects and clients: - Allow them to somehow change the package you are offering - Instead of pressuring them, offer them options on what to do next - Give them the opportunity to remove options/features from your offer - Make it safe for them to take the next step - Give them two options so that they do not feel pressured - Try to involve other people in the conversation - Let them believe that they know more than you think they know about your product
C Styles

C-style Prospect - Motto: “If we do not have time to do it right, do we have time to do it over again?” - As a result, C-styles are good at ensuring quality control. - Focus: Analyze tasks and things. - Under Pressure: Overly critical. - This refers to C-styles have a tendency to be so focused on the details that they often find mistakes and errors. The other styles may find C-styles too critical. - Fear: Criticism of work. - This refers to C-styles' want to be correct and to produce high-quality work. - They do not want to make mistakes. - Favorite question: Why? (Why does is work this way? Why should we do it?)

C-Style Prospects - Communication Style: - Better in written communication - Doesn’t express disagreeing views - Includes a lot of facts and details - May miss the big picture - Doesn’t talk about opinions or abstract matters - Extremely diplomatic

C-Style Prospects - When communicating with a C-style prospect, remember to: - Tell them something they already know and make them believe they know the rest as well - Allow them to think they are in control - Be careful not to go into unnecessary details with them - Feed them with ideas and possibilities - Make yourself their friend - When you go into details, remember not to get bogged down in them - Always paint the big picture before going into the details

C-Style Prospects - Tips on how to develop the relationship with a C-style client: - Let them participate in the quality control - Regularly ask for their feedback - Be enthusiastic and friendly, but at the same time detailed - Make them a professional expert in the eyes of their own organization - Give them a small personal discount - Make them realize they have made the right decision - Get them to benefit from you

C-Style Prospects - What not to do with C-style prospects and clients: - Avoid formal negotiation settings that would put them in the spotlight - Do not be arrogant by trying to show you have superior knowledge about their area of expertise If you have never done this before, do not let them know it - Do not confuse them with too many choices - Do not cover all their questions thoroughly; only the ones that are actually relevant - Do not bring up details that do not support you achieving your goals - Do not lead or manipulate them into situations they might not feel safe and secure

C-Style Prospects - Moving the business relationship forward with C-style prospects and clients: - Offer them an option to retreat back if they fear they have committed to too much too soon - Stay calm and show that you have done this many times before - Make placing an order as easy as possible - preferably online or written - Do not pressure them, yet do not delay the question "are you ready to buy" - Formalize the status of your friendship - Try to get them to talk themselves into a decision - Promise something additional in after-sales service

M-120: Using AI to Help You Sell

A Fundamental Paradox - "All technology that has ever existed or will ever exist that is meant to help salespeople will ultimately be rendered useless by those same salespeople—with full support of their leadership."

What AI Misuse Looks Like in Sales - Avoiding Discomfort - Template Dependency - Generic Positioning - Scaling Mediocrity - Using AI to bypass the challenging aspects of selling rather than sharpening your skills in those areas - Over-reliance on pre-built templates, automation, and surface-level prompts that sound generic - Communications that sound like Sales 101 textbook examples instead of reflecting deep knowledge of your specific buyer - Using AI to shortcut thinking processes, effectively automating and multiplying average-quality output
Bad questions yield bad answers. - ...in sales and in AI.

How AI Really Works - AI is not inherently intelligent—it predicts what should come next based on patterns it has observed. - It doesn't know your specific buyer, sales process, or business context - It can't create true insights without your expertise as input - The more precise and detailed your input, the more valuable and differentiated the output

If You Don't Give It Context... - "It gives you the world's context." - The Generic Email Opener - The Empty Check-In - The Timid Request - "Hope this email finds you well..." - "Just checking in to see if you've had a chance to review..." - "Let me know if now's a good time to connect..." - When you provide vague instructions to AI, it defaults to the most common patterns in its training data—the same tired phrases every average salesperson uses.

Example: Prompt with vs. without Context - Prompt A: Generic - Prompt B: Specific - "Write a follow-up email." - "Write a 2-sentence follow-up to a CFO at a $20M manufacturing company who showed interest in retention and hasn't replied in 6 days." - Results in generic, forgettable content that sounds like every other sales email in your prospect's inbox. - Creates targeted, contextual content that demonstrates understanding of the buyer's specific situation. - Reflect: Which example aligns with your current approach? Which email would compel your buyer to reply?

AI Follows Systems - Defined Process - System Scaling - Input Quality - Not a Creator - AI excels at executing and scaling your well-defined sales processes. - It can multiply the effectiveness of your existing sales system. - Garbage in = garbage out (at impressive scale and speed). The quality of your input directly impacts AI's output. - AI cannot invent effective systems from scratch. It relies on your strategy and framework. - The key insight here is crucial for your success: AI isn't a replacement for a structured sales methodology. Instead, it's a powerful multiplier for whatever system you already have in place. How well-defined are your current sales processes?

Your Job: Coach the Tool - Revise Aggressively - Never accept the first draft—your expertise is crucial to refine AI output and turn it into something truly impactful. - Experiment & Iterate - Actively experiment by changing tone, trying new angles, simplifying language, clarifying points, and injecting your unique insights. - Maintain Control - Remember, AI is your powerful assistant, not a replacement for your judgment. You remain the decision-maker and the owner of every client relationship.

The Cost of AI Misuse - Invisible Mediocrity - You sound average in a sea of average, making it impossible to stand out and win deals - False Confidence - You believe you're leveraging cutting-edge AI when you're actually reinforcing outdated approaches - Skill Atrophy - Your core selling skills stagnate while your competitors continue developing theirs alongside AI

The Consequence Matrix - Uses AI Well - Misuses or Ignores AI - Strong Seller - Weaponized Edge - Gets Left Behind - Struggling Seller - Polished Faker - Invisible - Where do you stand? - The most dangerous position is the "Polished Faker" who uses AI to sound better without actually developing deeper expertise. They initially appear competent but quickly reveal their lack of substance when challenged. Take a moment to reflect on your current approach and identify your position within this matrix.

Use Case 1: Prep Smarter - ChatGPT + Perplexity AI - Rapidly research company background and current market context - Develop deeper understanding of buyer's likely priorities and pain points - Create comprehensive pre-call strategy in under 90 seconds - The result: You enter calls with the contextual knowledge that typically requires hours of research, allowing you to ask more insightful questions and demonstrate relevant expertise.

Prompts to Use for Pre-Call Prep - These prompts are designed to help you quickly gather intelligence and develop a comprehensive understanding before your sales calls. Use them in your AI tool of choice to accelerate your research process. - Company-Specific Research - Role & Industry Understanding - Competitive Landscape - "What's happening at [Company] right now that would affect [department]? Include recent news, earnings calls, and strategic initiatives from the past 6 months." - "What does a [title] at a [company type] usually care about in [industry]? Include typical KPIs, challenges, and career progression concerns." - "What solutions is [Company] likely using for [function], and what are the common complaints about those solutions in this specific industry?" - Why it works: This prompt helps you identify current business priorities, potential triggers for change, and relevant initiatives. Understanding the company's recent activities allows you to connect your solution directly to their strategic goals, making your outreach highly relevant. - Why it works: Beyond company-specific details, this prompt helps you grasp the individual's world. Knowing their KPIs, common challenges, and career aspirations enables you to frame your message in terms of personal and professional gain, building stronger rapport and trust. - Why it works: This prompt provides crucial insights into the competitive environment and potential pain points with existing solutions. Armed with this knowledge, you can strategically position your offering by highlighting your unique differentiators and addressing common frustrations head-on.

Use Case 2: Message Testing - Elevate Your Communications with ChatGPT - Tone Analysis - Test how your message sounds in terms of confidence, clarity, and buyer-centric framing - Template Transformation - Convert generic templates into sharp, personalized positioning that stands out - Value Proposition Testing - Refine and pressure-test your 30-second commercial for maximum impact

Prompts to Improve Your Messaging - Confidence Calibration - Audience Adaptation - Objection Anticipation - "Make this message less needy and more confident while maintaining a collaborative tone. Remove any language that undermines my expertise." - "Rewrite this opener for a skeptical VP of Operations who is primarily concerned with efficiency and risk reduction." - "What objections might a smart buyer raise to this proposal, and how should I preemptively address each one without being defensive?" - The most powerful aspect of AI message testing is the ability to quickly iterate through multiple versions before sending anything to a prospect.

Use Case 3: Objection Practice - Ready to sharpen your skills? This section focuses on leveraging AI for practical sales training. - AI Roleplay Tools for Skill Development - Benefits of AI-Powered Practice: - Practice difficult conversations privately without judgment - Simulate realistic resistance, pressure, and emotional responses - Receive immediate feedback on tone, pacing, and word choice - Test multiple approaches to the same objection to find what works best

AI doesn't replace you. It reflects you. - If you're sharp, it sharpens you. - If you're vague, it embarrasses you. - AI amplifies your existing expertise, allowing you to scale your best thinking and deepest industry knowledge across more prospects and opportunities. - AI exposes mediocre thinking by producing generic, templated content that prospects immediately recognize as inauthentic and low-value. - Be the seller who uses AI to think better—not to think less.

Reflection Prompt - "AI will help me sell better by ___________." - Take a moment to write down your specific answer, considering the unique challenges in your sales process where AI could provide the most leverage.

Understanding Motivation
How do you define “Motivation”?
[Image only]
Types of Motivation

Intrinsic Motivation - Behavior that is driven by internal rewards. In other words, the motivation to engage in a behavior arises from within the individual because it is naturally satisfying to you. - Examples: Improving skills, Being your best, something to prove, etc

Extrinsic Motivation - Behavior that is driven by external rewards. These rewards can be tangible. - Examples: Money (items you can purchase with Money), Scores, Grades, or intangible, such as praise or fame.

Altruistic Motivation - Motivated by a desire to impact others, even at a detriment to themselves. (e.g., to encourage a change in another's approach to life; to boost others' confidence or empower them to take charge of their lives). - Example: Giving your jacket and shoes to a homeless person.
What can happen if you don’t understand which type of motivation fits each person and align to it?
Performance Motivators
Relationship - Need for friendly relationships - Are motivated by interactions with other people
Status - Need to be effective, influential and to make an impact - Strong need to get their ideas across - Increasing their status and prestige is important
Achievement - Need for sense of accomplishment - Seek the attainment of realistic yet challenging goals - Have a strong need for feedback - See ways to do things better

The Rules - for giving concessions - Never make concessions unless you know the buyer’s compelling reason (interests) AND their specific requests/demands and why they MUST be met. - Never concede unless you get a concession in return. - Do not accept the buyer’s first attempt at getting a concession. - Articulate the value of any concession you make.

The Facts - regarding giving concessions - Large concessions indicate that the first number was very far off from the “real” number, and that the buyer is still far from the bottom line. - Rapid/Large concessions also undermine the credibility of the salesperson. - Small concessions indicate that you are close to the “real” number. - All concessions teach that more concessions can and will be made.

The Art & Science - of giving concessions - Give concessions slowly. - Give concessions in small pieces. - Make it appear to hurt. - Get something of equal or greater value to you. - Never answer an unasked question. - Use silence strategically.

KEY CONCEPT #2 - Under pressure, you will default to what you are most comfortable with.

The Rules - Giving Concessions - Never make concessions unless you know the buyer’s compelling reason (interests) AND their specific requests/demands and why they MUST be met. - Never concede unless you get a concession in return. - Do not accept the buyer’s first attempt at getting a concession. - Articulate the value of any concession you make.

The Facts - Giving Concessions - Large concessions indicate that the first number was very far off from the “real” number, and that the buyer is still far from the bottom line. - Rapid/Large concessions also undermine the credibility of the salesperson. - Small concessions indicate that you are close to the “real” number. - All concessions teach that more concessions can and will be made.

Art & Science - Giving Concessions - Give concessions slowly. - Give concessions in small pieces. - Make it appear to hurt. - Get something of equal or greater value to you. - Never answer an unasked question. - Use silence strategically.

Selling Value

Qualifying

Qualifying: - Meets with Decision Makers - Uncovers Actual Budget - Will Discuss Finances - Knows Decision-Making Process - Can Influence the Decision-Making Process - Handles High-Ticket Pricing OK - Need to Be Liked Doesn't Get in the Way - Able to Stay in the Moment - Self-Limiting Beliefs Won't be an Obstacle - Knows Why They Would Buy - Asks about Everything - Not Vulnerable to Competition
Presentation Approach

Presentation - Approach: - Emphasizes Listening over Talking - Able to Minimize Talking about Company - Products or Solutions - Not Compelled to Present - Not Overly Reliant on Educating and Presenting - Does Not Believe Presenting Equates to - Controlling the Sales Process - Does Not Believe Making A Proposal is the Most - Important Part of the Sales Process - Not Compelled to Propose or Quote - Asks Enough Questions - Takes Nothing for Granted
Closing

Closing: - Gets Prospect to Agree to Make a - Decision - Will Meet with the Decision Maker - Will Find a Way to Close - Not Likely to Take "Think it Overs" - Unlikely to be Derailed by Put-Offs - Manages Appropriate Amount of - Patience - Closing Urgency - Isn't Hoping to be Liked - Will Stay in the Moment at Closing Time - Won't Make Inappropriate Quotes

Negotiating

Sales Posturing

Working Remotely

UN-079: Negotiation Competencies - Willing to Walk - Presented by: Rob

Strategies for Effective Negotiation and Conflict Resolution - Via Chris Voss - No is a starting point, not a rejection - No creates safety and control for the other person and opens up real dialogue. - Practice tactical empathy - Understand and acknowledge the other person's feelings and perspective without needing to agree. - Use mirroring and labeling - Mirror: Repeat the last few words they said. Label: Identify their emotions with phrases like 'It sounds like...' or 'It seems like...' - Ask calibrated questions - Use open-ended 'How' and 'What' questions to shift problem-solving to the other person. - Avoid splitting the difference - Compromise often leads to subpar outcomes—aim for creative, collaborative wins. - Conduct an accusation audit - Proactively list potential objections or negative assumptions to neutralize them upfront. - Control your tone - Use the calm, slow 'late-night FM DJ' voice to create trust and calm tense situations. - Aim for 'That's right,' not 'You're right' - 'That's right' signals they feel deeply understood. 'You're right' often ends the conversation without agreement. - Give the illusion of control - Let them feel like they're steering the conversation while you guide the outcome. - Be strategic with time and deadlines - Use time and deadlines to your advantage in negotiations.

Negotiation Competency - Seeks win/win - Focuses on mutually beneficial outcomes, where both parties feel satisfied with the resolution. - Willing to walk - Understands when to walk away from a negotiation that is not aligned with their goals or principles. - Appropriate amount of patience - Demonstrates patience and resilience, allowing the negotiation process to unfold naturally and avoiding rash decisions. - Listens & asks with ease - Actively listens to the other party, asking thoughtful questions to better understand their needs and concerns. - Remains present - Stays focused and engaged throughout the negotiation, avoiding distractions and maintaining a professional demeanor. - Goal oriented - Keeps the end goal in mind, aligning their actions and strategies to achieve the desired outcome. - Problem solver & diagnostician - Approaches challenges with a solutions-oriented mindset, identifying and addressing the root causes of issues. - Need for approval - Maintains a level of self-confidence and resilience, not solely dependent on the approval of others. - Rejection-proof - Handles rejection and setbacks with composure, using them as opportunities for growth and improvement. - Sells on value - Focuses on highlighting the value and benefits of their offering, rather than engaging in a price war. - Discusses finances in depth - Demonstrates a strong understanding of financial considerations and is comfortable delving into the details of a deal.

D-style - Motto: I did it my way. - Focus: Actively controls tasks and things. - Under Pressure: Lack of concern. - This refers to D-styles’ tendency to overlook how their actions and behaviors affect others. - Fear: Loss of control. - This refers to D-styles’ desire to be in charge. They do not want to give up control. - Favorite question: What? (What is the bottom line? - What is in it for me?)

I-style - Motto: "I am a nice person. Everyone should like me." - Focus: Actively involved with other people and emotions - Under Pressure: Disorganized - This refers to I-styles' tendency to focus so much on people that they may overlook details and tasks. - Fear: Social rejection - This refers to I-styles' having a strong desire to be liked by others. - Favorite question: Who? (Who is going to be at the meeting? Who else is using this?)

S-style - Motto: "If it's not broken, let's not fix it." - Focus: Involved with familiar people. - Under Pressure: Too willing. - This refers to S-styles’ have a tendency to be accommodating and polite. Often they say “yes” too easily. - Fear: Loss of stability. - This refers to S-styles wanting to have a stable and secure environment. Change can be challenging for S-styles. - Favorite question: How? (How are we going to do this? How does this impact us?)

C-style - Motto: “If we do not have time to do it right, do we have time to do it over again?” - As a result, C-styles are good at ensuring quality control. - Focus: Analyze tasks and things. - Under Pressure: Overly critical. - This refers to C-styles have a tendency to be so focused on the details that they often find mistakes and errors. The other styles may find C-styles too critical. - Fear: Criticism of work. - This refers to C-styles' want to be correct and to produce high-quality work. - They do not want to make mistakes. - Favorite question: Why? The Anatomy of Discomfort
Growth Lives on the Edge

Comfort Reaction | What It Looks Like | Growth Move - Fixing for them | "I'll just take care of it." | "What do you see as your next step?" - Over-empathizing | "I get it, it's a tough week." | "Yes, and what's the plan to recover?" - Avoiding tension | "Skipping 1:1s, sugar-coating feedback." | "Deliver clarity with calm - not comfort." - Lowering standards | "Let's just get through this month." | "Recommit to the process, not relief."
Leading Discomfort on Purpose
Healthy Pressure
“You’re doing well — and I think there’s another level here we haven’t touched yet.”
“I’m not going to lower the bar; I’m going to help you rise to it.”
“Let’s stay here until it feels natural — that’s how we know it’s working.”
It’s NOT criticism, micromanagement, or perfectionism.
It matters because - Comfort creates a plateau. - Chaos creates burnout. - Intentional tension creates adaptation.
Why is works - It builds self-trust - It hardwires confidence - It replaces external pressure with internal drive
Your job isn’t to make people comfortable. - It’s to make them capable.
The Fix
Set a clear standard — and stop moving it.
Replace relief with reflection.
Coach to the edge, not over it
Celebrate endurance, not escape
Model it yourself
“You did the uncomfortable thing. That’s the real progress I care about.”

The Manager Evidence Standard
1. The Problem - Described a specific current-state problem. - Explained where or when it occurs. - Identified who or what is affected.

2. Business Impact - Lost or delayed revenue. - Increased cost. - Wasted time or capacity. - Customer loss or dissatisfaction. - Employee turnover or burnout. - Operational risk. - Missed goals. - Compliance or reputational exposure.

3. Personal Impact - Stress or frustration. - Lost credibility. - Increased workload. - Pressure from leadership. - Risk to performance goals. - Inability to focus on more important priorities. - Career or reputational consequences.

4. Cost of Inaction - The financial impact continuing. - A customer leaving. - A deadline being missed. - Growth being restricted. - Employees continuing to leave. - An executive goal remaining unmet. - The buyer continuing to absorb the personal consequences.

5. Commitment to Change - Establishing a real timeframe. - Giving access to affected stakeholders. - Providing requested information or data. - Assigning internal ownership. - Scheduling a defined next step. - Investing meaningful time or resources. - Agreeing to resolve an identified obstacle. - Prioritizing the issue against competing initiatives.
